newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Rage at peace failure sparks new Arab uprising.
newsitem.headline: Rage at peace failure sparks new Arab uprising.

text.p: Palestinian frustrations over a foundering peace process and deteriorating living conditions boiled over into the anti-Israeli uprising that spread across PLO-ruled areas this week.

The Palestinian uprising, or intifada, that erupted nine years ago was triggered by a car accident in the Gaza Strip. But it gave vent to rage over the Israeli occupation and despair at the lack of a solution.
This time, Israel's opening of a tunnel near Islam's third holiest shrine, al-Aqsa mosque in Jerusalem, ignited angry protests across the West Bank and the Gaza Strip and in Arab East Jerusalem.
Palestinians assailed the Israeli step as an assault on their holy sites and an attempt to Judaise Jerusalem.
Israeli troops have shot dead 44 Palestinians and Palestinian forces have killed 11 Israelis in two days of clashes that started on Wednesday. Palestinians call it the "al-Aqsa massacre."
In the uprising launched in 1987, then-Defence Minister Yitzhak Rabin tried unsuccessfully to quell the intifada through force and a policy of breaking arms of Palestinian stone-throwers.

"By using more force than Rabin to quell the spirit of the new intifada, Netanyahu is trying to show he can do better, but our people will not be stopped," said Abdel-Jawwad Saleh, Palestinian agriculture minister and legislator.

Palestinian youths and old men and women, some carrying their babies in their arms, rushed towards Israeli soldiers at an army roadblock between the West Bank city of Ramallah and Jerusalem, indifferent about the possibility of being shot.
Protesters recalled national slogans of the Palestinian revolution calling for armed struggle and threw stones at Israeli soldiers who responded by opening fire at the crowds.

"There is a revival of the intifada. The people are ready to defend Jerusalem and their lands and to confront the Israelis on the field regardless of sacrifices, and indifferent to the large numbers of victims," Saleh said.
Youths defied Palestinian police orders to withdraw to Ramallah, away from Israeli gunfire.
"This is a revolution, we have had enough of Israelis humiliating our dignity and denying us our rights," said Abu Youssef, 54. "They have made us feel the bitterness of peace."

"Where is this peace? We believed we would have better living conditions, we would have freedom and independence, but what we got was closures, the worst economic conditions and a new kind of occupation," said Mustafa, 23.
Palestinians celebrated in the streets of the West Bank and Gaza Strip when the 1993 PLO-Israel peace deal was signed in Washington.
High hopes were dampened as Palestinians realised they were still controlled by Israelis, despite the evacuation of Israeli troops from parts of the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
Conditions worsened when Israel sealed PLO-controlled areas following a series of suicide attacks by Moslem militants opposed to the peace deal in Israel that killed 59 people.
"We have nothing to lose. If Israel wants to continue controlling us, we are ready for war, otherwise we must be given our rights," a young protester said.

Anger at Palestinian President Yasser Arafat's Palestinian Authority for failing to get Israel to adhere to peace agreements shifted to support when Palestinian policemen clashed in gunbattles with Israeli soldiers.
Even Palestinian policemen were frustrated with what they viewed as an "illusionary" peace.

"Peace deal or not, we can't stand by and watch our people get massacred. We will kill those who spill our people's blood," said one policeman who rejected his commander's orders to stop shooting. "This peace has not offered us anything anyway."
